page_hint: Ch 20 §1 'Concept' (opening paragraph) vs §3 'Fleet aggregate throughput (illustrative form)' and the 'Reading Fig 20.1's two gaps' paragraph
quoted_clause: The central insight is that aggregate system throughput is not merely the sum of individual host throughputs; it is modulated by scheduling overhead, network contention, and the cost of moving data between hosts and storage.
observed: The chapter's stated central insight is never demonstrated or quantified. The worked example's model is exactly a sum, Λ_fleet = N × Q, with a single scalar efficiency derate; the figure note explicitly disclaims the modulation ('Queueing and tail-latency penalties are not determined by this two-line calculation and must be shown separately if claimed'). The reader is promised a non-additive effect and given an additive model.
evidence: §3: 'Λ_fleet = N × Q'. Fig 20.1 note: 'Queueing and tail-latency penalties are not determined by this two-line calculation and must be shown separately if claimed.' §4 measures the effects (dispatch latency, utilization variance) but never connects them back to the aggregate-throughput claim.
root_cause: The Concept section was written as a general statement about fleet behavior; the model that followed was a capacity screen, and the two were never reconciled.
correction: Either (a) add one quantified modulation term to the model — e.g. show that at the canonical 40 rps the fleet's aggregate admitted rate is below N × 1.977 once per-host utilization variance and dispatch delay are included, using the Table 20-1 targets (dispatch p99 < 100 ms, utilization CV < 0.2) as the inputs — or (b) restate §1's insight as the scope of the model: 'the additive screen is a first-order capacity floor; the non-additive effects (scheduling, contention, data movement) are real but are not captured by it and are measured in §4'. Option (b) is cheaper and honest; option (a) is stronger.
acceptance_test: §1's central claim is either demonstrated with a number or explicitly scoped to the model actually used, and the reader is not left believing the additive screen captures fleet effects.

page_hint: Ch 20 §7 'What We Still Don't Know', bullet 'Economic auto-scaling'
quoted_clause: A fleet that runs at 20% utilization on average may be cheaper in the cloud; one at 80% utilization favors owned hardware. The transition point is a function of capital expenditure amortization period, electricity cost, and the volatility of user demand.
observed: The chapter already contains the numbers needed to compute the own-vs-cloud crossover and does not do so: §3 gives $20/hr cloud and $8/hr amortized owned per host, which fixes the crossover at 40% utilization (8/20). The bullet instead asserts two example utilizations and then lists the transition point as unknown, when the chapter's own inputs determine it for the canonical host.
evidence: Owned $8/hr vs cloud $20/hr: owned is cheaper when 8 < 20 × u, i.e. u > 0.40. At u = 0.20, cloud effective cost = $4/hr < $8/hr (cloud wins, as the bullet says); at u = 0.80, cloud effective = $16/hr > $8/hr (owned wins, as the bullet says). The crossover is 40%.
root_cause: The bullet was written as an open question without noticing that §3 had already supplied the two cost constants needed to close it for the canonical host.
correction: Compute the crossover explicitly with the chapter's stated constants and label it [DERIVED] from [ILLUSTRATIVE] inputs: 'for the canonical 8×H100 host, the amortized-owned fleet ($8/hr) beats on-demand ($20/hr) above 40% sustained utilization; the true crossover moves with the amortization period, electricity cost, and demand volatility, which are not specified here.' Then the genuine open question is the volatility/over-provisioning term, not the base crossover.
acceptance_test: The bullet states a computed crossover with its inputs, and the residual uncertainty is limited to the terms the chapter cannot supply.

page_hint: Ch 20 §3, subsection heading 'Call this quantity what it is — one phrase, used identically in Chapters 16, 17 and 20'; and the parenthetical in the preceding subsection

evidence: Quoted above; the parenthetical appears in the 'KV-residency / latency bound' subsection and points forward to a heading whose own text is meta.

correction: Rename the heading to a reader-facing claim, e.g. 'What the ~2.0 req/s figure is — and is not'. Replace the parenthetical with a plain forward reference: 'a **KV-slot upper bound on admitted rate** (defined below)'. page_hint: Ch 20 §3, 'Fleet aggregate throughput (illustrative form)' and the 'correct statement' paragraph; §8 mini-case table and bullet (c)

page_hint: Ch 20 §5 'Common Mistakes', bullet 'Ignoring cold-start cost'
quoted_clause: loading the full model weights into HBM takes 30–120 seconds [ILLUSTRATIVE] (a load-path assumption for a ~140 GB model over a ~10–40 Gb/s (≈1.25–5 GB/s) path — 140 GB ÷ 30–120 s ≈ 4.7–1.2 GB/s, i.e. ≈37–9 Gb/s — not a hardware benchmark
observed: The stated load-time range and the stated path range are not mutually consistent at the endpoints: at the top of the path (40 Gb/s = 5 GB/s) the load takes 140/5 = 28 s, below the stated 30 s floor; at the bottom of the path (10 Gb/s = 1.25 GB/s) it takes 140/1.25 = 112 s, below the stated 120 s ceiling. The parenthetical's own arithmetic (4.7–1.2 GB/s = 37–9 Gb/s) puts the low end at 9.3 Gb/s, i.e. below the 10 Gb/s path minimum it is supposed to be consistent with.
root_cause: The 30–120 s range was chosen first (as a plausible figure) and the path range was back-fitted, so the endpoints do not close.
correction: Make the range derive from the path: 'over a ~10–40 Gb/s path, a ~140 GB load takes ~28–112 s (≈37–9 Gb/s of sustained effective load rate)'. Or keep 30–120 s and widen the path to ~9–40 Gb/s. Either way the two ranges must be consistent at both endpoints.
acceptance_test: The load-time range and the path range are mutually consistent at both endpoints when recomputed from 140 GB.

page_hint: Ch 20 §5 'Common Mistakes', bullet 'Overlooking data movement cost'
quoted_clause: If every host pulls data independently, the network cost scales linearly with fleet size. A better approach is to colocate vector stores with serving hosts or use a shared cache layer that amortizes fetch cost across concurrent queries.
observed: The stated contrast is vacuous as written: per-host network cost is constant regardless of fleet size, so total network cost necessarily scales linearly with fleet size under any scheme. The sentence therefore does not distinguish the two architectures it is meant to compare.
evidence: The distinguishing quantity is bytes moved per query (and hence aggregate egress), not the scaling exponent: independent pulls move N × (context bytes) per query-batch; a shared cache moves (distinct context bytes) once per distinct context, amortized across concurrent queries.
root_cause: The bullet was phrased as a scaling claim rather than as a bytes-per-query claim.
correction: Restate in terms of the quantity that differs: 'independent pulls move the retrieved context once per query per host (≈ context bytes × queries); a shared cache moves each distinct context once and serves subsequent hits locally, so the saving is proportional to the cross-query context-overlap rate'. Then quantify with the canonical context size (the retrieved portion of the ~9,200 in-tokens) so the reader can size the saving.
acceptance_test: The bullet's contrast is expressed in a quantity that actually differs between the two schemes (bytes per query or egress), not in a scaling exponent that is identical for both.

page_hint: Ch 20 §8 mini-case, bullet 'Algebra practice (kept [ILLUSTRATIVE])'
quoted_clause: **Algebra practice (kept [ILLUSTRATIVE]):** the per-host 250 rps / fleet 2,000 rps arithmetic is kept only to show the *structure* of the fleet math (marginal host cost ÷ marginal capacity): $20 ÷ 250 = $0.08 per rps per hour. The 250 rps is hypothetical and unachievable for this 9.2K-in/300-out workload

A skimming reader can easily carry away '$0.08 per rps per hour' as the marginal cost, which the very next sentence says is not the answer.

root_cause: A pedagogical aside retained from an earlier draft without re-evaluating whether it earns its place in the finished mini-case.

If a hypothetical is retained for teaching purposes, move it to a clearly marked footnote and use a rate within one order of magnitude of the derived bound (e.g. 20 req/s) so the arithmetic does not imply a plausible-but-wrong figure.
acceptance_test: The mini-case contains no number that a reader could mistake for the chapter's answer, and no editorial justification for keeping a passage.

page_hint: Ch 20 §3, 'Fleet aggregate throughput (illustrative form)', displayed equation
quoted_clause: Λ_fleet = N × Q
observed: The symbol Λ is used for a capacity rate while λ is used throughout the chapter (and in Little's Law) for the arrival rate. Two visually similar symbols for different quantities in the same subsection invites misreading, particularly in the sentence that follows ('At the canonical peak of 40 rps, fleet size must satisfy both the KV-residency and the throughput/latency bounds').

page_hint: Ch 22 §3 (Table 22-1, 'decode weight-read per token' and 'decode weight-read BW rate' rows); §3 Step 4; §6 first paragraph; §8 mini-case
quoted_clause: decode weight-read per token | ~140 GB | full-weight-read model (70B FP16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] ... decode weight-read BW rate | ~5.6 TB/s | ~140 GB / 25 ms TPOT (= traffic / decode interval)
observed: The table and the surrounding prose present '~140 GB per token' and '~5.6 TB/s' as per-token/per-request decode quantities without stating that they are batch-size-1 figures. Weight traffic per decode step is ~140 GB regardless of batch size; it is amortized across the batch, so per-token weight traffic is ~140/B GB at decode batch B. The canonical operating point (10 rps average, 25 ms TPOT) implies a decode batch well above 1, so the per-token figure overstates the actual per-request weight traffic by roughly the batch factor.
evidence: Per-step weight read = 70B params x 2 B = 140 GB, independent of batch. At the canonical 25 ms TPOT and a per-host step time of ~5.2 ms (140 GB / 26.8 TB/s aggregate HBM on 8xH100), a host sustains ~191 steps/s; at 12,000 output tokens/s (40 rps peak) the required batch is ~4 per host. Per-token weight traffic is then ~35 GB/token, not 140 GB/token, and the required aggregate read rate is ~1.4 TB/s, not 5.6 TB/s. The 5.6 TB/s figure is the batch-1 upper bound. The book's own arithmetic elsewhere (Ch 6 arithmetic intensity ~1.0 FLOP/byte) is a per-step property and is unaffected.
root_cause: A per-step quantity is labeled and propagated as a per-token quantity. The 'full-weight-read model' label names the mechanism but does not state the batch assumption, and the table's 'per token' column header makes the wrong reading the natural one.
correction: In Table 22-1, rename the rows to 'decode weight read per step (batch-independent)' and 'decode weight-read rate at batch size 1', and add a note: 'at decode batch B the per-token weight traffic is ~140/B GB and the required aggregate read rate is ~5.6/B TB/s; the 5.6 TB/s figure is the batch-1 upper bound and the decode-bandwidth conclusion in Ch 6 holds because arithmetic intensity (~1 FLOP/byte) is far below the H100 machine balance (~295 FLOP/byte) at any batch.' Apply the same qualifier in §3 Step 4, §6 and the §8 mini-case.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '140 GB' and '5.6 TB/s' in Ch 22 states the batch assumption, and Table 22-1's row headers no longer imply a per-token reading. A reader can state the batch-1 vs batch-B relationship without consulting another chapter.

page_hint: Ch 22 §8 mini-case, paragraph beginning 'The peak, not the average, sizes the fleet'
quoted_clause: a homogeneous cluster sized at ~16 hosts clears both budgets and avoids duplicated model residency and KV-transfer cost
observed: The ~16-host figure is derived from prefill FLOPs only (51.5 PFLOP/s at 40 rps peak / 3.16 PFLOPS per host at 40% MFU = 16.3 hosts). The claim that this sizing 'clears both budgets' is asserted without a decode-side or KV-capacity derivation, and the KV check that the chapter's own Table 22-1 enables is marginal under the canonical assumptions.
evidence: KV capacity check (canonical 8xH100 SXM 80 GB host = 640 GB HBM; 140 GB weights; ~500 GB for KV): 500 GB / 24.1 GB per request (Table 22-1) = ~20.7 concurrent requests per host; 16 hosts = ~332 concurrent requests. Required concurrency at the 40 rps peak = 40 rps x (1.08 s prefill + 300 x 25 ms decode = 8.58 s service time) = ~343 requests. 332 < 343, i.e. the 16-host sizing is ~3% short on KV capacity before any activation/workspace allowance. Decode-side check: 12,000 output tokens/s at 40 rps peak needs ~63 steps/s fleet-wide at batch 4, well within HBM capability, so decode is not the binding constraint - but this is never shown.
root_cause: The mini-case sizes the fleet from one resource dimension (prefill FLOPs) and then generalizes the result to 'both budgets', skipping the KV-capacity dimension that the chapter itself tabulated two pages earlier.
correction: Add the KV-capacity and decode-side arithmetic to the mini-case: state the per-host KV budget (640 GB - 140 GB weights = ~500 GB), the resulting concurrency per host (~20 requests at 24.1 GB/request), the required concurrency at the 40 rps peak (~343), and the resulting host count (~17-18 hosts at the canonical 24.1 GB/request, before activation headroom). Then state the conclusion as 'sized at ~16-18 hosts for prefill and KV, with decode not binding', and note that the fleet's 21 hosts carry the redundancy margin.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's host count is derived from at least two resource dimensions (prefill FLOPs and KV capacity), and the phrase 'clears both budgets' is either supported by shown arithmetic or removed.

page_hint: Ch 21 §8 mini-case, final sentences
quoted_clause: The candidate is rejected automatically, the incumbent stays, and the legal subset keeps working. No fire drill, no user-visible regression, no manual heroics - the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business
observed: The mini-case's own numbers contradict its closing claim. It states the canary served 12 legal-subset failures - i.e. 12 real user requests received a wrong answer - and then asserts 'no user-visible regression' and 'cost nothing to the business'. The canary's blast radius was not zero; it was bounded and small.
evidence: 12 legal-subset failures out of ~360 legal-subset canary requests = ~3.3% observed failure rate on that subset, versus the incumbent's ~0.83%. Those 12 requests were served by the candidate and were user-visible failures. The chapter's own §3 framing ('a controlled ~3.6K-request canary') is the correct framing; the closing sentence overstates it.
root_cause: Rhetorical closure substituted for the chapter's own quantitative claim. The mini-case ends with an absolute ('nothing', 'no user-visible regression') where the mechanism delivers a bounded, quantified reduction.
